question.problem: What is the coefficient of ${(x-\frac{1}{6})}^{2}$ in the second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)$ at $x=\frac{1}{6}?$
question.worked_solution:
The second-degree Taylor polynomial of $f(x)$ about $x=\frac{1}{6}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{2}(x) & =f(\frac{1}{6})+{f}^{′}(\frac{1}{6})(x-\frac{1}{6})+\frac{{f}^{″}(\frac{1}{6})}{2}{(x-\frac{1}{6})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The coefficient of ${(x-\frac{1}{6})}^{2}$ in the above Taylor polynomial is 

$$
\frac{{f}^{″}(\frac{1}{6})}{2}.
$$

To find this coefficient, we start by computing the second derivative ${f}^{″}(x):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x) \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) \\ {f}^{″}(x) & =-{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we evaluate ${f}^{″}(x)$ at $x=\frac{1}{6}.$ This gives

$$
{f}^{″}(\frac{1}{6})=-{\pi }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})=-{\pi }^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}=-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2}.
$$

Finally, we determine the coefficient of ${(x-\frac{1}{6})}^{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{f}^{″}(\frac{1}{6})}{2} & =\frac{(-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{2})}{2}=-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$
